item.title: Monitoring Linux - Metrics and Log Forwarding - v26.10.2 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
- New: the Host page's Kernel tab shows the hardware's temperature and the processor's thermal throttling, and the Alert Catalog has a Host hardware running hot template - Bug fix: in a row of single values, a title that wrapped to more lines than its neighbours' pushed its value below theirs Collectord updates: - New (beta): `[output.otlp]` sends logs and metrics over OTLP/HTTP or OTLP/gRPC to an OpenTelemetry Collector or a backend that takes OTLP, alone or beside the Splunk output; `continuesFrom = splunk` carries the file and journal positions over when the receiver forwards into the same Splunk, an `[output.splunk::otlp]` section must be renamed, as the OTLP output takes that name, and a release before this output refuses `defaultOutput = otlp` - New (beta): `[output.s2s]` sends events and metrics-index records to Splunk indexers over Splunk-to-Splunk (Splunk 9.1 or later), with indexer acknowledgements, TLS, optional compression and indexer discovery; `continuesFrom = splunk` carries the file and journal positions over when S2S replaces HEC for the same Splunk, and an `[output.splunk::s2s]` section must be renamed, as the S2S output takes that name - New: with several Splunk HEC `urls`, Collectord moves to the next one every `loadBalanceFrequency` (5 minutes by default), with `ackEnabled = true` as well, so the load spreads across the HEC endpoints again after they restart one by one; `loadBalanceFrequency = 0` moves only after a failure, as before - New: on physical machines the host stats report the hottest temperature sensor, how close a sensor is to its limit, and how often the processor throttled for heat (`temperature_max_celsius`, `temperature_margin_celsius`, `thermal_throttle_core_events_per_sec`, `thermal_throttle_package_events_per_sec`); virtual machines have no sensors and report none - Updated Go runtime to 1.27.4 - Updated SQLite Library to 3.54.1 - New: a client certificate (`clientCertPath`, `clientKeyPath`) or CA bundle (`caPath`; not yet the S2S output's, which needs a restart for a new CA) replaced on disk, such as a renewed certificate in a mounted Secret, is used for new connections within a minute, without restarting Collectord; a replacement that cannot be loaded keeps the previous one and logs a warning - New: `maxConnAge` in `[output.splunk]` and `[output.otlp]` sets how long the output's connections take requests before Collectord opens new ones, so DNS or a load balancer that balances connections can pick another endpoint for a Collectord instance that would otherwise stay on the one it first reached; unset, connections are not replaced by age, as before, and it does not apply with `ackEnabled = true` - Bug fix: Collectord could take too long to stop, and be killed, when its destination did not answer - Bug fix: when Splunk HEC answered 503 "Server is busy" after taking part of a batch, the events it had taken were indexed twice - Bug fix: events were lost without a warning when the Splunk HEC `url` answered with a redirect to a page that returns 200, such as the sign-in page of an SSO gateway in front of it; the events are now held and retried - Bug fix: TLS connections through some firewalls, such as Palo Alto Networks, were reset or timed out - Bug fix: a burst of records for an output other than the pipeline's own, such as the metrics-index copies `indexType = both` sends to `metricsOutput`, could be dropped (`multioutput_dropped_events`) while that output was still taking them - Bug fix: `timestampPrecision` of 7 to 9 on the Splunk HEC output sent rounding noise in the last digits of an event's time; it now sends the event's exact digits


Short Description:
See your Linux servers in Splunk: the systemd journal with each entry's unit named, log files, failed units and pending updates, and host, process, network, filesystem and disk stats in an events or a metrics index. Dashboards for hosts, services, inventory and network, and 45 alert templates. Install one package on each host from our signed apt and yum repositories.


Description:
Monitoring Linux brings your Linux servers into Splunk: the hosts your services run on, from RHEL and its rebuilds, Debian and Ubuntu to Fedora, Amazon Linux 2023 and SUSE, on amd64 and arm64. A service fails and systemd restarts it in a loop, and nobody notices. A host slows down, and nobody can tell whether it is CPU, memory pressure, I/O or one runaway process. A filesystem fills up, the connection tracking table fills and the kernel drops new connections, or security updates wait for weeks on a host nobody remembers. The answers sit in each host's journal and /proc, one host at a time. Monitoring Linux shows what Collectord forwards from each host. Collectord runs as a systemd service and sends the journal, the log files under /var/log and your applications' own log files to a Splunk events index, with the systemd unit of every journal entry and every process named, so a log line or a CPU spike is one search away from its service. It also reports the units in the failed state every minute and the pending package updates every hour. Host, process, network, filesystem and disk stats go to the same events index or to a Splunk metrics index, your choice: the app has a set of dashboards for each, and they look the same. The dashboards start from Hosts: one row per host with its CPU, memory, load and stall, and the alerts that fired. From there they go to one host in depth, its processes, the fleet's inventory and pending updates, the systemd services that failed, restart or were OOM-killed with their logs a click away, the network's interfaces, connections and listening ports, filesystems and disk I/O. Give each group of hosts a cluster name, such as prod or staging, and the dashboards and the Alert Catalog filter by it. Alerts come from an Alert Catalog of 45 templates, written for Splunk admins, the platform team, security and application teams. Each team picks the alerts it needs and creates them as its own saved searches, scoped to its own clusters. For Splunk Enterprise Security, the app maps SSH logins, sudo, host performance, inventory and pending updates to the Common Information Model. Install the collectorforlinux package on each host from our signed apt and yum repositories, or the tarball on any other distribution, set the HEC URL, token and license key in 002-user.conf, and enable the service. Upgrades keep your configuration. The app goes on your search heads, on Splunk Enterprise 9.2 or later or Splunk Cloud Platform. The app requires Collectord and a license key from Outcold Solutions. Evaluation and developer keys are free. Documentation: https://www.outcoldsolutions.com/docs/monitoring-linux/

Short Description:
See your Docker, Compose, Swarm, Podman and Amazon ECS hosts in Splunk: container and host logs and Docker events in an events index, host, container and process stats in the events index or a metrics index. Dashboards that lead to what needs fixing, and 61 alert templates each team scopes to its own clusters. One Collectord container per host.


Description:
Monitoring Docker brings the hosts that run your containers into Splunk: Docker hosts and Compose projects, Docker Swarm clusters, Podman hosts, and Amazon ECS container instances. Containers fail in ways their logs alone don't explain. A container restarts in a loop, is OOM killed, or fails its health check. A Swarm service runs fewer tasks than it should, and the reason is in the Swarm's services, tasks and nodes, which only a manager can read. The Docker data root fills up with images, writable layers and json-file logs. Some containers run their processes as root or hold Linux capabilities. The answers are spread over every host, in the logs, the cgroups, /proc and the Docker API. Monitoring Docker shows what Collectord forwards from each host, where it runs as one container. Collectord sends container and host logs, the Docker daemon's events, and the containers, images, volumes and Swarm objects it reads from the API to an events index. Host, container, process, network, filesystem and disk stats go to the same events index, to a Splunk metrics index, or to both while you compare. The containers of rootless Podman users are monitored too. The app opens on an Overview that says whether anything needs attention and where: hosts whose stats went silent, Collectord problems, and containers OOM killed, in a restart loop, unhealthy or exited with a non-zero code. From there it drills down to hosts, containers and processes, Compose projects, Swarm services and nodes, ECS services, privileged containers, the network, filesystems, disk I/O and CPU throttling. Every stats dashboard has a twin that reads the metrics index, and the Configuration page chooses which set the menu shows. Name each cluster, such as prod or staging, and the dashboards and alerts filter by it. Alerts come from an Alert Catalog of 61 templates, written for Splunk admins, the platform team and application teams. Each team picks the alerts it needs and creates them as its own saved searches, scoped to its own clusters. Container labels configure one container at a time: its index and Splunk output, field extraction, multi-line events, masking, log files from its volumes, and Prometheus endpoints. Three features, off by default, send fewer events: repeated lines as one counted event, storms of alike lines folded into a summary a minute, and a report of each stream's heaviest log patterns. Install the app on your search heads, create an HTTP Event Collector token, and start Collectord on each host with docker run, Docker Compose, a Swarm stack, Podman, or an Amazon ECS daemon service. The app requires Collectord and a license key from Outcold Solutions. Evaluation and developer keys are free. Documentation: https://www.outcoldsolutions.com/docs/monitoring-docker/

an object without its own token is now refused (its workloads fall back to the default output, with a warning), and one with its own `url` sends only there, without indexer acknowledgements, which Collectord logs once where `ackEnabled = true` - Bug fix: `collectord verify` reported the POST checks as FAILED for a Splunk output with `compressionLevel = nocompression`, though Collectord delivered to it - Bug fix: Prometheus could not scrape Collectord's `/metrics/prometheus` endpoint and reported the target down when an `[input.kubernetes_watch::*]` input watched an API group other than the core one (on OpenShift the shipped `clusterresourcequota` watch does), or one namespace with a `-` in its name: the input's counter had the `.`, `/` or `-` in its name; each is now `_`, as in `openshift_watch_quota_openshift_io_v1_clusterresourcequota__count` - Bug fix: a pod whose workload is owned by a cluster-scoped object (on OpenShift the DaemonSets of the DNS and Network operators) was missing that owner's id, labels and annotations, and Collectord asked the API server for the owner, and was answered 404, each time such a pod changed; a 404 for an owner deleted before its pods is now remembered for five minutes instead of asked for again on each change


Short Description:
See your OpenShift clusters in Splunk: container logs, the journal, audit logs, events and objects, with node to process stats and control-plane metrics in an events or a metrics index. An Overview that leads to the cause, an Audit menu, and 117 alert templates. Install Collectord with one Helm chart; a Red Hat certified image is available.


Description:
Monitoring OpenShift brings your OpenShift clusters into Splunk: for the platform team that runs them, the application teams that deploy to them, and the security team that audits them. When a release goes wrong on OpenShift, the evidence is spread out: container logs on every node, the journal, events the API server keeps for about three hours, the audit logs of four API and OAuth servers, and the control plane's Prometheus endpoints. On a cluster many teams share, each team also needs its own data and its own alerts, and the platform team needs rules that hold for every project. Monitoring OpenShift shows what Collectord forwards from each cluster. Collectord runs as a DaemonSet on every node, masters included, and one addon pod. It sends container and application logs, the journal, the audit logs, and OpenShift events and objects to an events index, and node, pod, container, process, network and disk stats and the control plane's Prometheus metrics to an events index or a Splunk metrics index. Annotations change what it does for one project, workload or pod: an index or a HEC token per team, field extraction, multi-line events, masking and hashing, application log files and Prometheus scrapes. A Configuration resource sets the platform team's rules for the whole cluster. New features, off until you turn them on, group repeated lines and fold storms of alike lines, for fewer events and less noise. The dashboards open on an Overview with one verdict for the fleet, Healthy, Warning, Critical or Unknown, the numbers behind it and a row per cluster, and its tiles and rows drill down to the page that shows the cause. From there they cover nodes down to a single process; crash loops, OOM kills and failing probes, each a click from the pod's logs; capacity, quotas and what the Pod specs declare; the API server, etcd and the cluster DNS; pod security posture; and an Audit menu from detections to the timeline of one object, OAuth logins included. The stats dashboards come in two sets that look the same, one for each kind of index. Alerts come from an Alert Catalog of 117 templates, written for Splunk admins, the platform team, security and application teams. Each team picks the alerts it needs and creates them as its own saved searches, scoped to its clusters and projects. Install the app on your search heads, then Collectord with one Helm chart or the manifest rendered from it, on OpenShift 4.11 or later. It sends to Splunk Enterprise or Splunk Cloud over the HTTP Event Collector. A Red Hat certified image is available from registry.connect.redhat.com, and FIPS 140 images are published beside the standard ones. The app requires Collectord and a license key from Outcold Solutions. Evaluation and developer keys are free. Documentation: https://www.outcoldsolutions.com/docs/monitoring-openshift/

an object without its own token is now refused (its workloads fall back to the default output, with a warning), and one with its own `url` sends only there, without indexer acknowledgements, which Collectord logs once where `ackEnabled = true` - Bug fix: `collectord verify` reported the POST checks as FAILED for a Splunk output with `compressionLevel = nocompression`, though Collectord delivered to it - Bug fix: Prometheus could not scrape Collectord's `/metrics/prometheus` endpoint and reported the target down when an `[input.kubernetes_watch::*]` input watched an API group other than the core one (on OpenShift the shipped `clusterresourcequota` watch does), or one namespace with a `-` in its name: the input's counter had the `.`, `/` or `-` in its name; Short Description:
See your Kubernetes clusters in Splunk: container and host logs, events, objects and the API audit log in an events index, and node, pod, container, process and Prometheus metrics in the events index or a metrics index. Dashboards that lead to the cause, and 118 alert templates each team scopes to its clusters and namespaces. Deploy Collectord with Helm or one manifest.


Description:
Monitoring Kubernetes brings your Kubernetes clusters into Splunk, for the platform team that runs them, the application teams that deploy to them, and security. When something breaks in a cluster, the evidence is spread out and short-lived: container logs sit in files on each node until rotation overwrites them, and the API server holds Kubernetes events for about an hour. Dashboards that only show state leave you to work out what is wrong. And when one cluster serves many teams, one fixed set of alerts fires the same way for everyone, while each team's data has to stay in its own indexes. Monitoring Kubernetes shows what Collectord forwards from each cluster. Collectord runs as a DaemonSet on the nodes, control-plane nodes included, and a single addon Deployment, and enriches what it sends with Kubernetes metadata. Container logs, application log files, host logs, and Kubernetes events and objects go to an events index, and so does the API server audit log once you turn it on. The node, pod, container and process stats, and the Prometheus metrics of the control plane and your own pods, go to the same index or to a Splunk metrics index, your choice. Annotations on a namespace or pod send its data to its own index and HEC token, join multi-line stack traces and mask values, and can send repeated lines as one event that counts them, for fewer events and less noise. The app opens on an Overview with one verdict for all your clusters, the numbers behind it and a row per cluster, and its tiles drill down to the page that shows the cause. From there it covers nodes, pods, containers and processes; the Kubernetes events, where a click on a crash loop or an OOM kill opens that pod's logs; capacity, requests and limits; the control plane from the API server to etcd and CoreDNS; pod security posture and network connections; and an Audit menu that reads the API audit log, from detections to the timeline of one object. Every stats dashboard comes in two sets that look the same, one for each kind of index. Alerts come from an Alert Catalog of 118 templates, written for Splunk admins, the platform team, security and application teams. Each team picks the alerts it needs, scopes them to its clusters and namespaces, and creates them as its own saved searches, such as Kubernetes: Pod crash looping [cluster prod; namespace payments]. Install the app on your search heads, create a HEC token, and deploy Collectord with the Helm chart or one manifest. It works with containerd, CRI-O and Docker on Kubernetes 1.24 and later, managed clusters such as EKS, GKE and AKS included. The app also maps your nodes and the API audit to the Common Information Model for Splunk Enterprise Security. The app requires Collectord and a license key from Outcold Solutions. Evaluation and developer keys are free. Documentation: https://www.outcoldsolutions.com/docs/monitoring-kubernetes/

Description:
Monitoring macOS brings your Apple Silicon Macs into Splunk: build and CI fleets, Macs that host virtual machines, and the laptops IT looks after. Macs are often the one part of an estate that Splunk cannot see. A build farm slows down and nobody can tell whether it is thermals, memory pressure, a full disk or one runaway process. A laptop fleet drifts out of policy, with FileVault off, updates pending or the firewall disabled, and the first sign is an audit. The unified log holds the answers, but it is too large to forward as it is, and most of it is noise. Monitoring macOS shows what Collectord forwards from each Mac. Collectord runs as a LaunchDaemon and sends hardware, power, process and security stats to a Splunk metrics index, and the unified log, crash reports, launchd services, logins and setting changes to an events index. Log packs choose what to forward from the unified log, and a rate cap and a noise sampler keep its volume in check. Apps fetch the labelled version with get_prompt() in the genai-telemetry SDK. * Agent & Tools dashboard: tool error rate and latency, agent run health, possible tool loops. **Other changes** * All navigation is in a left sidebar on every page; Splunk's app bar is hidden. The sidebar can be collapsed to a slim rail (« button or the \[ key). * Load demo data button creates realistic sample traces, sessions, scores, prompts and a dataset, so you can try the app without your own data (admin role needed). * Time to first token: uses the real ttft_ms value when the SDK sends it. * Time-based model pricing: add a dated row to genai_model_pricing_history.csv when a price changes, so past costs stay correct. A nightly search rebuilds the current-price lookup. * Four alerts (cost spike, error rate, P95 latency, token budget) with volume floors so they stay quiet until real traffic flows. * GenAI_Traces data model gained session, user, trace name, prompt, environment, release, TTFT, tool and agent fields. * Light and dark themes; filters and time range are kept in the page URL so views can be bookmarked. **Upgrade notes** * Use genai-telemetry 1.3.0 or later for nested traces, sessions, users, inputs/outputs and scores. Trace, evaluate and improve LLM apps in Splunk: nested traces, sessions, users, scores, datasets and prompt versions, plus cost, latency and error dashboards.


Description:
GenAI Observability for Splunk monitors GenAI and large language model applications by collecting and analyzing trace data for requests, latency, token usage, cost, errors, retrieval-augmented generation retrieval, and agent tool calls. The app ingests trace telemetry into custom indexes and provides trace exploration pages modeled , dashboards for performance and cost management, and a Python SDK for instrumenting applications. item.title: TA-sensors - v1.0.1 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Short Description:
Collects Linux hwmon (lm-sensors class) board health - CPU/core temperatures, fans, voltages, NVMe temps, power - from BMC-less hosts with zero dependencies. Stdlib python3 reads /sys/class/hwmon and emits JSON events, mstats-ready sensors.* metrics, and dashboards.


Description:
TA-sensors brings hardware health monitoring to the machines IPMI can't reach. Consumer desktops, gaming rigs, VMs, SBCs and other BMC-less hosts have no out-of-band management controller, so server-grade hardware telemetry (temperatures, fans, voltages, power) is invisible to Splunk. The Linux kernel already exposes all of it through the hwmon subsystem under /sys/class/hwmon - TA-sensors collects it natively, without a BMC, without ipmitool, and without even the lm-sensors package. Two stdlib-only python3 scripted inputs collect every registered hwmon chip (coretemp/k10temp, acpitz, nvme, r8169, mt7921, amdgpu, vendor drivers, and more): - sensors:status (index=main): one nested-JSON event per cycle with sensor_name, reading, reading_value, units and status for every sensor, including latched _alarm flags. - sensors:metrics (index=metrics): true metric events via METRIC-SCHEMA, named sensors._, ideal for mstats time-series, anomaly alerts and trend dashboards. Milli-scaled sysfs inputs are normalized (temp/in/power/current/humidity /1000, fan raw rpm), duplicate chip names are disambiguated with their hwmon number, and all names are sanitized so metric names stay clean and dashboard-safe. Included dashboards: Sensors Overview (per-host reporting, current readings, alarm table) and Sensors Metrics (CPU cores, temperatures, fans, voltages, power draw, live metric volume). TA-sensors is fully standalone, but pairs with TA-IPMI, which covers BMC-equipped servers - together they give complete hardware observability across a mixed fleet. Free and source-available for personal, educational and evaluation use; commercial use requires a paid license from BentleyPC LLC (see LICENSE).

item.title: CJIS Compliance App - v1.2.0 [New App Release]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
\# CJIS Compliance App 1.2.0: Release Notes Covers everything changed since version 1.0.22. \## Summary (short form for the Splunkbase release notes field) 1.2.0 makes the app safe to trust out of the box and much more useful day to day. Every control now starts as "not assessed" instead of pre-marked. Findings no longer flood or duplicate. A new Setup and Data Readiness page shows what data the app is missing. Nine new dashboards add triage, incident logging, a policy-area scorecard, a gaps list, encryption in transit, network boundary, remote access, vulnerability and patch status, and source investigation. Detections were tightened, and in-app documentation was expanded. Requires the Splunk Common Information Model (CIM) add-on. \## New dashboards \*\*Compliance\*\* \- \*\*CJIS Policy Area Scorecard:\*\* posture and findings rolled up to the 13 CJIS Security Policy areas (5.1 to 5.13), with a click-through to each area's controls. \- \*\*Gaps and Actions:\*\* controls that are not implemented, with owner, due date and days overdue, plus controls whose review is overdue. \- \*\*Incident Log:\*\* an append-only record of reportable incidents and whether and when each was reported to the state CJIS Systems Agency (CJIS 5.3, NIST IR-6). \- \*\*Evidence Pack:\*\* one page for an auditor: posture summary, every control with status and findings, audit retention against your requirement, weekly snapshots and status history. Export to PDF or CSV. \- \*\*Setup and Data Readiness\*\* (first item in the menu): shows, for each CIM data model, whether it is accelerated and has data, which controls have the data they need, which scope lists are still empty, and which indexes are searched. \*\*Monitoring\*\* \- \*\*Encryption in Transit (SC-8 / SC-13):\*\* allowed connections over protocols that do not encrypt traffic, with a "what to fix" recommendation for each, and weak TLS versions when certificate data is present. \- \*\*Network Boundary (SC-7):\*\* allowed versus blocked traffic, reachable services, top blocked sources and ports, and firewall changes. \- \*\*Remote Access (AC-17):\*\* remote logons, most active remote users, failed logons by source, and users signing in from more than one country. \- \*\*Vulnerability and Patch Status (SI-2 / RA-5):\*\* open critical and high vulnerabilities, how long they have been open, and failed or pending updates. \*\*Investigation\*\* \- \*\*Finding Triage (IR-4 / IR-5):\*\* acknowledge, assign, close or mark a finding a false positive, with a note and a full history of who changed what and when. \- \*\*Source / IP Investigation:\*\* logons, firewall traffic, intrusion signatures and findings for a single address. \## Improvements \*\*Trustworthy defaults\*\* \- Every control now ships as \*\*not assessed\*\*. Nothing is pre-marked as implemented. \- Control status changes are recorded with who and when. The posture editor requires an owner and accepts an optional due date. \- A weekly \*\*Evidence Snapshot\*\* search records each control's status and findings over time (off by default). \*\*Findings\*\* \- Each condition is now \*\*one finding\*\* (for example, one source failing logons) that is updated on each run, with first seen and last seen times. Previously a persistent condition added a new finding every hour. \- Triage decisions are stored separately, so re-running a search never undoes them. \- Findings are kept for a configurable number of days (default 365). \*\*Detections\*\* \- \*\*Brute force then success:\*\* now checks that the success came after the failures. It replaces the separate Cross-System Correlation search, which duplicated it. \- \*\*Privileged group membership (AC-6):\*\* now works with classic Windows event logs, which it previously missed, and covers more groups plus removals. \- \*\*File integrity (SI-7):\*\* limited to watched locations (system files, startup and autorun keys, services) and ignores known noise, so it no longer floods. It stays off until you supply Sysmon data and change windows. \- \*\*Log source silent (AU-5):\*\* per-source limits, and silent hosts on the CJIS device list. \- \*\*Malicious code (SI-3):\*\* uses the CIM Malware data model instead of one vendor's data. \- \*\*MFA (IA-2):\*\* uses the CIM Authentication data model. \- \*\*Configuration changes (CM-3):\*\* reports changes outside approved change windows. \- \*\*New: cleartext protocols (SC-8):\*\* creates findings for high-risk unencrypted protocols such as FTP, Telnet, POP3, IMAP and LDAP without TLS. \- \*\*Account exclusions:\*\* machine and Windows system accounts are ignored by default, and you can add your own service accounts in \`cjis_account_exclusions_local.csv\`. \- The after-hours window, brute-force threshold and silent-source limit are now settings you can change. \*\*Dashboards and documentation\*\* \- Dashboards no longer show machine-account and logoff noise in the account-change and privileged-logon tables. \- Menu names now include their control numbers. \- New in-app documentation: Getting Started, Using Finding Triage, Using the Incident Log, Scorecard / Gaps and Actions / Evidence Pack, Monitoring and Investigation Pages, and a Settings Reference. \## Upgrading from 1.0.x \- \*\*Findings:\*\* findings written by earlier versions used a different key. After upgrading, old findings remain until they age out and can appear next to new ones. If you want a clean start, you can clear them by running \`| inputlookup cjis_findings | where 1\=0 | outputlookup cjis_findings\`. This deletes all findings. \- \*\*Control status:\*\* your existing status records are kept. Only new installs start as "not assessed". \- \*\*Lookup files:\*\* Splunk keeps existing lookup files when an app is upgraded, so new rows in shipped CSVs do not appear on upgrade. Replace the file if you want them. \- \*\*New settings (macros):\*\* \`cjis_findings_retention_days\`, \`cjis_required_retention_days\`, \`cjis_review_interval_days\`, \`cjis_bf_threshold\`, \`cjis_silent_default_minutes\`, \`cjis_after_hours_start\`, \`cjis_after_hours_end\`, \`cjis_fim_scope\`, \`cjis_fim_noise\`, \`cjis_remote_access_filter\` and \`cjis_exclude_accounts\`. Defaults are in the Settings Reference. \## Requirements \- Splunk Enterprise or Splunk Cloud Platform 9.x or 10.x, on a search head. \- The Splunk Common Information Model (CIM) add-on with the data models you use (Authentication, Change, Intrusion_Detection, Network_Traffic, and optionally Malware, Vulnerabilities, Updates and Certificates). Accelerate the models for speed. The Setup and Data Readiness page tells you which are missing. \## Known limitations \- The finding triage and incident log pages write to the KV store, so Splunk shows a one-time "risky commands" warning. Review the search and choose Run Query Anyway. \- A closed finding stays closed if the same condition happens again. Check its last seen time and reopen it if needed. \- SI-7 needs Sysmon file and registry events and real rows in \`change_windows.csv\`. \- Status is a self-assessment by your team. The app records and reports it but cannot prove a control is implemented. \- Multi-agency scoping is not included in this release. \- Protocol detection in Encryption in Transit is by port number, so services on non-standard ports are not classified.


Short Description:
CJIS Compliance maps the FBI CJIS Security Policy v6.0 to NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5. It tracks which controls are implemented, monitors security data through CIM, and stores correlation findings for review without Enterprise Security.


Description:

Posture covers the 13 CJIS policy areas. Each control can be marked implemented, partial, planned, not assessed, or not applicable.

item.description:

Release Notes:
Please provide a read-only API token for the Cloudflare account whose audit logs Splunk will collect. Grant Account / Account Settings / Read, and limit the account resource to the specific account. Supply its Account ID and send the token through our approved secret-sharing channel. If client-IP filtering is enabled, allow the actual outbound IPs of our Splunk collector. No write permission or Global API Key is requested." WHY THIS PERMISSION This TA calls GET /client/v4/accounts/{account_id}/audit_logs. The endpoint lists Account Settings Read or Account Settings Write as accepted permissions. Choose Read for least privilege; Write is not necessary for this integration. Source: Cloudflare's account audit log API reference: [https://developers.cloudflare.com/api/resources/audit_logs/methods/list/](https://developers.cloudflare.com/api/resources/audit_logs/methods/list/) Do not substitute Access: Audit Logs Read. That permission covers Cloudflare Access authentication logs, not the account audit endpoint used here. Zone / Logs / Read and Logpush permissions are not required for this TA's request. Permission definitions: [https://developers.cloudflare.com/fundamentals/api/reference/permissions/](https://developers.cloudflare.com/fundamentals/api/reference/permissions/) TOKEN SETUP 1\. An authorized Cloudflare user opens My Profile > API Tokens > Create Token and creates a custom token. Token creation does not give that user access to accounts or privileges they did not already have. 2\. Set policy type Account, permission Account Settings, access Read. 3\. Limit Account Resources to the account(s) authorized for collection. Prefer a dedicated token scoped to the single account for each input. 4\. Choose an expiry/rotation policy. If IP filtering is used, allow the actual collector egress IPs. The Splunk Web hostname's DNS address is not evidence of its outbound/NAT IP. Obtain Cloud egress information from your Splunk administrator or support team. 5\. Store the displayed secret securely. Enter it directly in the TA's Bearer Token field. Do not include "Bearer ", quotes or surrounding whitespace. 6\. Use the 32-character Account ID, not a Zone ID or account display name. Cloudflare also offers account-owned tokens. Use them only after confirming support for this endpoint and your organization's token-creation policy. Neither a Cloudflare password nor a Global API Key is accepted by this TA. Instructions and resource scoping: [https://developers.cloudflare.com/fundamentals/api/get-started/create-token/](https://developers.cloudflare.com/fundamentals/api/get-started/create-token/) VALIDATE THE ACTUAL ACCESS Saving the Splunk form validates its format and securely stores the token; it is not proof that Cloudflare authorized retrieval. Enable one input and check for "Cloudflare poll completed" in the internal logs. HTTP 200 with success\=true and result\=\[] means no records were returned. HTTP 401/403 means the credential/access checks above still need review. Token validity alone does not prove permission to the requested account. This release uses the v1 account endpoint, not the separate v2 /logs/audit, organization audit-log or Zero Trust Access authentication-log APIs.

Description:
TrackMe Broker lets TrackMe on Splunk Cloud reach the systems on your own network: remote Splunk instances (Heavy Forwarders, Deployment Servers), self-managed Cribl Leaders and webhook receivers. From a Splunk Cloud stack those destinations cannot be reached, because the stack cannot connect into your network. TrackMe Broker reverses the direction. This add-on runs on a Heavy Forwarder on your side, asks the stack for work over its REST API on port 8089, makes the HTTPS call locally and posts the answer back. Every connection starts on your side: you open nothing inbound. - Deny by default: the forwarder reaches only the targets you declare on it, whatever the stack asks for. - Encrypted end to end: each request and response is sealed for one paired forwarder (AES-256-GCM, keys on P-256), on top of HTTPS. - Paired, not trusted blindly: you accept each forwarder in TrackMe after checking its key fingerprint. - Highly available: run two forwarders in one broker; they share the work, and one carries on if the other stops. - Least privilege, FIPS-approved cryptography: the add-on authenticates with an account holding only the trackme_broker role. Requires TrackMe 2.4.24 or later on the stack. Documentation: https://docs.trackme-solutions.com/product_guide/integ_broker.html

item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
\- The field map tool generates maps for Windows Security as classic text (\`WinEventLog:Security\`), FortiGate and Palo Alto Networks, beside Windows Security as rendered XML and CloudTrail. With a FortiGate map, the Network_Traffic data model, \`tstats\` and the Splunk Security Content (ESCU) detections give the same results as on raw events. With a Palo Alto map, the Network_Traffic and Change data models, \`tstats\` and ESCU detections give the same results on compact PAN-OS traffic and system events as on raw ones; threat events are passed whole. \- The field map's \`check\` also counts the compact events indexed without their fields and those Splunk dropped because it could not load the map's lookup file, and fails with the count. When its probe arrives late, \`check\` keeps the template list unless Splunk's log shows events of the map dropped. The new Field Map Dropped Events alert reports dropped events by node every five minutes. \- The new search report, \`bin/tenx_search_report.py\`, reads a search head's saved searches, alerts and dashboards and says which run unchanged when a source moves to compact events, which need \`tx\`, \`txf\` or a field map, and which meet a limit the README states. The report changes nothing and starts no search. \- Word searches through \`tx\`, dashboards and compiled alerts find the events of every stored template, including templates stored in the last few minutes. Outside \`NOT\`, a wildcard inside a word (\`Se\*Privilege\`), \`TERM()\` of part of a longer term and \`CASE()\` of a word with a wildcard inside it match as on the original lines. \- \`tx\` and \`txf\` expand an event whose values begin or end with white space or a carriage return, such as a Windows event with CR LF line ends, to its full text, and a carriage return inside an event comes back in place. \- \`tx\` expands events whose template appears twice in the indexers' copy of the template collection. An event \`tx\` cannot expand keeps its compact text and says why in \`tenx_expand_refused\`. \- The Consume KV search stores every template record indexed since the last one it stored, a burst of new templates included, and its first run after an install or an upgrade reads every template record in the index. \`tx\` and \`txf\` warn when Consume KV failed, is still loading, or has not run for fifteen minutes. \- Alerts compiled in the Compile Alert view find their events when the scheduler runs them, including events of templates whose hash contains \`$\`. The recompile pass rewrites alerts compiled with an earlier version within 15 minutes of the upgrade, unless someone has edited them since. \- An epoch-seconds timestamp with a fraction, such as \`msg\=audit(1723042099.699:13369)\`, expands as written and sets the event's time. \- Beside a heavy forwarder, the Receiver can write compact events to files that the heavy forwarder reads and sends to the indexers with its own outputs, with no HTTP Event Collector or token. The \`\_indexers\` package gives each event back its host, source, index and time, and field maps run on the heavy forwarder. \- \`tx\` expands the events a FortiGate field map leaves under the compact sourcetype, such as FortiGate lines the add-on does not type, and a field map keeps the time of an event marked \`tenx_time\=sender\`. \- \`tx\` and \`txf\` run inside \`| union \[...]\`, in a search, a dashboard panel and a saved search, as they do inside \`multisearch\`, \`append\` and \`join\`. \- A search that holds more than one \`tx\` or \`txf\`, such as two arms of a \`multisearch\` or \`union\`, finds every event of each arm. \- \`| tx\` and \`| tenxsearch\` return their events inside \`append\`, \`join\` and \`union\`, and an unexpected error shows on the search instead of an empty result. \- Requires the Log10x Receiver at release 1.1.181 or later and Splunk Enterprise 9.4 through 10.6. After upgrading where a field map is installed, give the role of the token \`activate\` and \`check\` use search access to \`\_internal\`, and schedule \`check\` every minute. A map that \`gen\` generates again after the upgrade can carry a new index-time rule; install both of its apps again whole before running \`activate\`.


Short Description:
Send Splunk the logs that sampling and filters keep out to fit the license, on that same license. Compact events take a fraction of the volume and expand back byte-identical at search time; classic dashboards keep their SPL, and one command covers the search bar, saved searches, alerts and the REST API.


Description:
With the Log10x App, Splunk can index compact log events and still search, chart and alert on the original lines. The 10x Receiver stores each event as a template hash plus the values that change, so a stream of repeated patterns takes less of the license. On the OpenTelemetry demo, Splunk's license meter counted 63.91% fewer bytes, encoded events and templates included, and every line expanded back byte-identical with the Receiver settings in the installation steps (measurement: https://github.com/log-10x/benchmarks/tree/main/splunk-license). The same license then holds more: sources that were sampled, filtered or kept out of Splunk to stay under the limit can come back, or the license can be smaller. To search by what the lines say, write the tx macro in front of an ordinary search: index=my_index `tx` "payment failed" NOT retry. It runs as native SPL in the search bar, Dashboard Studio, saved searches and alerts, and NOT, OR, groups, phrases, field conditions, and values such as IP addresses and hostnames behave as they do on the original data. Classic dashboards keep their SPL: the browser sends each panel's search to the app, which rewrites it on the server. An alert created in the app's Compile Alert view is compiled once into a native saved search. The 10x Receiver produces compact events, and it is free on up to 10 nodes (https://www.log10x.com/pricing). No sign-up is required: with no license token it runs the full product on up to 10 nodes, air-gapped, with no expiry (https://doc.log10x.com/manage/license/). The app itself is open source under the MIT license.
